back: A build-up of electric charge that stays in one place on an object, usually caused by rubbing two insulators together.

front: What moves when objects become charged by rubbing?
back: Electrons (negative charges). Positive charges don't move.
Gaining electrons makes an object negative. Losing electrons makes it positive.
Like charges repel; unlike (opposite) charges attract.
The flow of electric charge around a circuit. Measured in amps (A) with an ammeter.
The "push" that drives the current (the energy given to the charges). Measured in volts (V) with a voltmeter.
How much a component opposes the current. Measured in ohms (Ω). More resistance means less current.

front: How are ammeters and voltmeters connected?
back: Ammeter: in series (in the loop). Voltmeter: in parallel (across the component).
Conductors let current flow (metals, graphite). Insulators don't (plastic, rubber, glass, wood).

front: Why must a circuit be complete?
back: Current can only flow around an unbroken loop. An open switch or a gap stops it.
The same everywhere, because there is only one path.
Shared between the components. The voltages add up to the battery voltage.
It splits between the branches, and the branch currents add up to the total current.
Each branch gets the full battery voltage.

front: What happens if one lamp breaks: series vs parallel?
back: Series: all the lamps go out. Parallel: the other lamps stay on.
Lamp: circle with a cross. Cell: long thin line and short thick line. Ammeter: circle with A.
